why: Counting with a frequency map plus an insight: reversing s[i..j] gives a new string exactly when the shortest such reversal has s[i] != s[j], and each distinct result corresponds to one pair (i, j) with different end letters. So the answer is 1 + the number of index pairs with different letters, computed from the 26 letter counts.
hints: If s[i] == s[j], reversing s[i..j] gives the same string as reversing s[i+1..j-1]. So which reversals are worth counting?
Claim: every pair i < j with s[i] != s[j] yields a distinct new string, and pairs with equal ends add nothing new. Plus the original string itself.
Pairs with different letters = C(n, 2) - sum over letters of C(cnt, 2). Answer = that + 1. O(n).
pitfalls: Do not forget the original password (reversing a length-1 substring).
The answer can exceed 32 bits for n = 10^5.
Enumerating substrings and hashing results is O(n^3); the count must come from the frequencies.
